n: Josiah becomes king as an eight-year-old boy after his father’s assassination and reigns thirty-one years (about 640–609 BC). He will become Judah’s great reforming king.

f.g: Her name means “beloved,” related to Solomon’s other name, Jedidiah.

n: Josiah is praised in the highest terms: he followed the Lord like his ancestor David and never swerved. Few kings receive such an unqualified compliment.

f.w: turned not aside to the right hand or to the left

n: In his eighteenth year (about 622 BC), when Josiah is twenty-six, he sends his royal secretary Shaphan to the temple to launch repairs.

f.g: The royal scribe or secretary of state; his family later protected the prophet Jeremiah (Jeremiah 26:24).

n: Shaphan is to have Hilkiah the high priest count the silver that temple doorkeepers had collected from worshippers for the repair fund.

f.g: Count or total up the money.
Priestly gatekeepers who received offerings at the temple entrance.

n: The money is to go to the supervisors of the work so they can pay laborers to repair the damaged temple—decades of neglect under Manasseh and Amon had taken their toll.
The funds will pay skilled tradesmen and buy timber and cut stone. The process echoes King Joash’s earlier temple repairs.

f.g: Stone cut and shaped for building.

n: The workers were so trustworthy that no one needed to audit them—a small but lovely note about integrity in God’s work.

During the work, Hilkiah discovers “the book of the law” in the temple—probably a form of Deuteronomy that had been lost or hidden during the wicked years. It shows how easily God’s word can be forgotten.

f.g: Many scholars identify it with Deuteronomy, whose covenant blessings and curses match Josiah’s reaction.

f.w: I have found the book of the law

n: Shaphan first gives the king a routine report on the repair funds before getting to the surprising news.
Shaphan mentions the book almost casually, then reads it aloud to the king. Hearing scripture read can change a life—and here, a nation.
Hearing God’s law, Josiah tears his clothes in grief—he realizes how far the nation has strayed from the covenant. His reaction shows a heart quick to repent.

f.g: Tore his garments, a traditional sign of mourning and distress.

n: The king sends a delegation of trusted leaders, including the high priest and the royal secretary, to seek the Lord’s will.
Josiah wants to know what God says about Judah’s situation. He accepts responsibility for the sins of past generations and fears the covenant curses written in the book.

f.g: Seek a revelation through a prophet.

f.w: great is the wrath of the LORD

n: The delegation goes to Huldah, a respected prophetess living in Jerusalem. That they consulted her, though Jeremiah was also active, shows her standing as a true prophetic voice.

f.g: Hebrew mishneh—“second quarter,” a newer district of Jerusalem, not a school.
Officer in charge of royal or priestly garments.

n: Huldah speaks plainly with the Lord’s authority, calling the king simply “the man that sent you”—before God, even kings are ordinary men.

f.w: Thus saith the LORD God of Israel
f.g: The classic formula of a prophet delivering God’s message word for word.

n: Her message confirms Josiah’s fears: the judgments written in the book will come upon Jerusalem.

f.g: Here meaning disaster or calamity, not moral wickedness.

n: The reason is the people’s long rejection of God for idols. The judgment is described as a fire that will not be put out.

f.g: Shall not be put out, like a fire that cannot be extinguished.

n: Huldah then turns to a personal message for Josiah himself.
Because Josiah’s heart was tender and he humbled himself and wept, God says, “I have heard thee.” Sincere repentance always reaches God’s ear.
Josiah will die before the disaster comes and will not witness it. Though he later dies in battle, he is spared the sight of Jerusalem’s destruction—the mercy that “in peace” promises.

f.w: gathered into thy grave in peace
thine eyes shall not see all the evil
